assessment: At the literal sentence level, the author groups pseudonyms and selective attribute disclosure together as functions the government confirms will arrive later. The original answer separates them: pseudonyms are deferred, whereas answers9a/d expressly describe selective release as working from the start. This is an affirmative textual tension, not merely missing evidence.

The strongest rescue is the paper’s narrower practical standard. Section3on7asks for selective attribute proofs across consumer applications, refers to the24-month issuer deadline and gives age/class-specific examples. Section7on9then expressly says the extent of data-minimising disclosure at launch is unclear and10demands full availability. The author may be objecting to complete implementation across issuers/use cases, rather than denying a base technical capability.

The government itself distinguishes infrastructure from issuer/acceptance readiness in answer4. Its guarantee of selective release does not guarantee every desired credential or attribute is issuable and useful at launch. That is a substantive benign interpretation; neither answer proves actual consumer-wide availability.

Zero-knowledge proofs, pseudonymous login, one-time credentials and selective disclosure are distinct; a counterexample concerning the first must not substitute for the last. No false claim is made that pseudonyms are promised at launch.

The explicit policy request to require privacy features from the beginning is grounded in7/9–10, but proof of a limited base function does not refute that broader request. If a narrow source-description finding is eventually retained, minor severity and cautiously conditional favourable direction fit better than major.

If the author’s sentence is explicitly defined elsewhere as all/complete consumer credential support, close the allegation; if an unqualified denial of base selective disclosure is established, a narrow attribution finding may survive.
